content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper focuses on extending graph convolutional networks (GCNs). The authors find that GCNs suffer from the over-smoothing problem, and they propose to solve it by using graph residual connections. The results on three datasets are promising.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
1. Over-smoothing is a major and common limitation of many GNNs, and the problem is worth studying.
2. This paper proposes a simple but effective method to alleviate over-smoothing in GCNs.
3. The results are promising.

Weaknesses:
1. Over-smoothing has been widely studied in the graph machine learning domain.
2. The idea of residual connections is not a new idea.
3. Only three small datasets are considered in the experiment.

I mainly have two concerns regarding the paper.
(1) The major idea of the paper is to use residual connections to solve the over-smoothing problem. However, this is not a new idea. For example, the idea has been explored by the following papers [1,2,3], which all introduce residual connections in GNNs. Although some model details might be different, I feel like they are very similar to this paper.
(2) In the experiment, only three small datasets (i.e., Cora, Citeseer, Pubmed) are used. All the datasets are very small, and the results might have high variance. Therefore, I would encourage the authors to report the standard deviation on these datasets and use some larger datasets for evaluation.

[1] Predict then propagate: Graph neural networks meet personalized pagerank
[2] Discrete and Continuous Deep Residual Learning Over Graphs
[3] Continuous Graph Neural Networks

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper proposes to step learning, a dedicated neural module that has an additional learning rate to control the decay rate of each residual block. Within this framework, the submission explores several different variants of residual connection. The submission evaluates the proposed method on standard benchmark such as cora, citeseer, and pubmed, and show that the proposed method is better than the vanilla implementation of residual connection, GCNII, and JKNet. 

The proposed method is novel but my concern is that the empirical evaluation is very small scale: only evaluating on the three smallest datasets and compare to two baseline methods. Unless the authors can improve these two shortcomings, my recommendation would be a rejection.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
## Strength
1. the proposed method is novel
2. the proposed method outperforms the baseline method of GRCN

## Weakness
1. The submission proposes several different variants of residual connection and unclear which is the recommended version
2. the experiments are only done on the three smallest graph benchmarks. I suggest carrying out experiments also on larger dataset such as the Reddit and/or the Amazon graph datasets.
3. The submission should compare to the more recent and state of the art methods. Some candidates are: pathGCN, EGNN
3.1 Question: Why is the accuracy of GCNII lower than that reported in the original GCNII paper? Is this due to difference in data split? I would suggest using the same data split as most prior works do

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper provides a new training pipeline for GCN and claims the proposed pipeline could relieve the over-smoothing problem.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Pros:
1. Compared to some baseline methods (JKNet[1] and GCNII[2]), the proposed StepGCN could achieve similar or better results on some benchmark datasets, such as Cora, CiteSeer and Pubmed.

Cons:
1. It is difficult to assess whether the proposed method solves or relieves the over-smoothing problem. In most cases, results of StepGCN are reported with just a few layers, e.g., two layers. It could be possible that StepGCN has a good ability to capture node characteristics rather than relieving the over-smoothing in deep GCNs. 

To better assess this, the authors should show how severe the over-smoothing is by tuning the number of layers in GCN and after adopting a step learning method, how this problem is alleviated. The assessment could follow a similar setting in [3]. It is suggested to adopt some metrices for assessing the over-smoothing, such as Mean Average Distance (MAD) [4]. 

2. Compared with state-of-the-art methods, the performance of StepGCN is not good enough. For example, the performance of SSP [5] and ACMII-GCN [6] on the Cora dataset is 90.16% ± 0.59% and 88.95% ± 1.04%, while that of StepGCN is 84.28%. Moreover, when compared with the Residual method GResNet [7], results of StepGCN are worse than those of GResNet reported in its original paper. For example, GResNet (GCN) on CiteSeer is 72.7%, while StepGCN gets 69.2% on CiteSeer.

References:
1. Xu, Keyulu, et al. "Representation learning on graphs with jumping knowledge networks." International conference on machine learning. PMLR, 2018.
2. Chen, Ming, et al. "Simple and deep graph convolutional networks." International Conference on Machine Learning. PMLR, 2020.
3. Lu, Weigang, et al. "SkipNode: On alleviating over-smoothing for deep graph convolutional networks." arXiv preprint arXiv:2112.11628 (2021).
4. Chen, Deli, et al. "Measuring and relieving the over-smoothing problem for graph neural networks from the topological view." Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence. Vol. 34. No. 04. 2020.
5. Izadi, Mohammad Rasool, et al. "Optimization of graph neural networks with natural gradient descent." 2020 IEEE international conference on big data (big data). IEEE, 2020.
6. Luan, Sitao, et al. "Is Heterophily A Real Nightmare For Graph Neural Networks To Do Node Classification?." arXiv preprint arXiv:2109.05641 (2021).
7. Zhang, Jiawei, and Lin Meng. "Gresnet: Graph residual network for reviving deep gnns from suspended animation." arXiv preprint arXiv:1909.05729 (2019).
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The step learning method proposed in the paper appears novel. The presentation of the paper is clear and easy to understand. 

There are some grammatical errors and typos in the paper. The authors should proofread and correct them.
content.summary_of_the_review: Though the step learning method improves over some GCN models, the authors should provide more evidence to support their claim that StepGCN could relieve the over-smoothing problem. The performance of StepGCN is not satisfactory: compared with SOTA methods, its performance is worse.

content.title: StepGCN: Step-oriented Graph Convolutional Networks in Representation Learning
content.abstract: Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) are employed to address a number of tasks in our society with their representation learning approach. Nonetheless, despite their effectiveness and usefulness, the majority of GCN-oriented approaches have an over-smoothing concern. Over-smoothing is the problem of node representations converging into a certain value, making the nodes indistinguishable. To effectively address the over-smoothing problem, we introduce StepGCN, a GCN model that integrates step learning techniques with graph residual connection networks. With our StepGCN, we achieved significant performance improvements in multiple representation learning benchmark datasets, and demonstrate that step learning can be expanded to other graph networks.
